This paper introduces a benchmark approach for the modelling of continuous, complete financial markets, when an equivalent risk-neutral measure does not exist. This approach is based on the unique characterization of a benchmark portfolio, the growth optimal portfolio, which is obtained via a generalization of the mutual fund theorem. The discounted growth optimal portfolio with minimum variance drift is shown to follow a Bessel process of dimension four.
The discounted GOP has the dynamics of a time transformed squared Bessel process of dimension four. The time transformation is given by the discounted underlying value of the GOP. The squared volatility of the GOP equals the discounted GOP drift, when expressed in units of the discounted GOP. ## Abstract
The paper proposes benchmark-neutral pricing and hedging for long-term contingent claims. It employs the growth optimal portfolio of the stocks as numéraire and the new benchmark-neutral pricing measure for pricing. For the assumed ‘natural’ dynamics of a well-diversified stock portfolio, which are those of the continuous limit of a branching process of diversified wealth in some activity time, this pricing measure turns out to be an equivalent probability measure. This is not the case for the putative risk-neutral pricing measure. Benchmark-neutral pricing identifies the minimal possible prices of contingent claims.

The paper introduces benchmark-neutral pricing and hedging for long-

keenable-realtime.snippet:
The paper treats the financial market as a communication system, using four information-theoretic assumptions to derive an idealized model with only one parameter. State variables are scalar stationary diffusions. The model maximizes the surprisal of the market and minimizes the Kullback–Leibler divergence between the benchmark-neutral pricing measure and the real-world probability measure. The state variables, their sums, and the growth optimal portfolio of the stocks evolve as squared radial Ornstein-Uhlenbeck processes in respective activity times.

Benchmark-neutral (BN) pricing, introduced in Platen (2025), uses the stocks' growth optimal portfolio (GOP) as numéraire and offers a practical, theory-based pricing approach.

The paper will show, under the MMM, the state variables, their aggregated sums, and the GOP of the stocks all evolve according to squared radial Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (SROU) processes as studied in Göing-Jaeschke and Yor (2003), each within their respective activity times. This result encapsulates the dynamic behavior of both individual and collective market components within an information-theoretic modeling context.

Under the BN pricing measure, the factors, sums of factors and the benchmark follow squared Bessel processes that evolve in respective observable activity times. Squared Bessel processes are special SROU processes, which were studied, for example, in Revuz and Yor (1999) and Göing-Jaeschke and Yor (2003). They are generalizations of the CIR process, which was popularized in finance in Cox et al. (1985). These processes are highly tractable with many explicit formulas for their functionals; see, for example, Baldeaux and Platen (2013).

Process benchmarking focuses on how activities are performed within an organization or compared to best-in-class peers. Instead of just the end results, the analysis asks: are there more efficient ways to achieve our goals?  
Benchmarking often reveals bottlenecks, inefficiencies, or gaps in the business process that waste resources or slow down improvement efforts. By examining both qualitative and quantitative data, organizations may find opportunities for streamlined operations or new tools to automate repetitive tasks.  
Operational efficiency thrives when benchmarking uncovers weak points in process or systems. This enables leaders to set realistic, data-driven goals instead of relying on abstract targets or outdated trends.
## Best Practices for Implementing Benchmarking Models  
Rolling out a successful benchmarking model requires preparation and an understanding of best practices. The process should fit your business goals and available resources.
### How can benchmarking software help?  
Benchmarking software automates data collection, analysis, and reporting, saving valuable time. With these tools, organizations can find, compare, and act on critical performance information much faster. This accelerates the improvement process and allows flexible use of different benchmarking models.

In this chapter, scalar- and multidimensional processes based on the squared Bessel process are discussed and subsequently applied in the context of the benchmark approach. In a first section, results from the literature regarding the squared Bessel process and related processes, namely the Bessel process, the square-root process, the 3/2 process and the CEV process are recalled. In the second part of the chapter, we introduce the Wishart process as the multidimensional generalization of the squared Bessel process. We remark that this process is revisited in Chap.
11, which is entirely devoted to this process. The chapter concludes by recalling from the literature a potential model for the Growth Optimal Portfolio, namely the Minimal Market Model. Formulated under the benchmark approach, the Minimal Market Model employs a squared Bessel process to model the Growth Optimal Portfolio. We demonstrate that an equivalent risk neutral probability measure does not exist for this model, yet the benchmark approach can still accommodate it. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the benchmark approach produces the same level of tractability as the Black-Scholes model. This chapter demonstrates that the benchmark approach can accommodate realistic, yet tractable models for the Growth Optimal Portfolio.

Abstract
This paper describes a two-factor model for a diversified market index using the growth optimal portfolio with a stochastic and possibly correlated intrinsic timescale. What did they find?

Here are the main results, explained simply:
* Normalized factors follow a special type of random process that stays positive and is pulled toward a typical level. In technical terms, they follow a Cox–Ingersoll–Ross (CIR) process in their own “activity time.” This choice comes from minimizing surprisal.
* The factors themselves, their sums, and the benchmark (the GOP of factors) follow squared radial Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (SROU) processes in their activity times. These processes are handy because they never go negative and have lots of known formulas, which makes calculations easier.
* The model, called the Minimal Market Model (MMM), has only one key parameter in market time: the net risk-adjusted return. That keeps it simple and reduces overfitting.
* Volatility spikes and “rough” behavior appear naturally because market time speeds up during hectic periods. This matches real markets much better than classic smooth models.

[View PDF](arxiv.org/pdf/2506.16264v1) [HTML (experimental)](arxiv.org/html/2506.16264v1)

> Abstract: The paper summarizes key results of the benchmark approach with a focus on the concept of benchmark-neutral pricing. It applies these results to the pricing of an extreme-maturity European put option on a well-diversified stock index. The growth optimal portfolio of the stocks is approximated by a well-diversified stock portfolio and modeled by a drifted time-transformed squared Bessel process of dimension four. It is shown that the benchmark-neutral price of a European put option is theoretically the minimal possible price and the respective risk-neutral put price turns out to be significantly more expensive.

The paper interprets financial markets as communication systems in the sense of Shannon's information theory. Trades and price evolutions reveal information at a variable intensity ("market activity"), naturally mapping to an activity time scale. The core modelling postulate is that scalar stationary diffusions , specifically squared radial Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (SROU) processes, serve as suitable state variables when viewed in market time. The separation of sources of randomness is achieved by representing stocks as portfolios of independent "factors," whose dynamics—normalized factors—are modelled using these SROU processes.

## Power Transformations in Stochastic Models

Take a stock price, square it, and ask what kind of process you are holding. The answer turns out to be surprisingly tidy: if the stock follows geometric Brownian motion, its square, its cube, its square root and its reciprocal all follow geometric Brownian motion too, just with a different drift and a different volatility. That single fact gives you every moment of a lognormal price in closed form, prices a whole family of \"power\" payoffs, and explains why a Monte Carlo estimate of a high moment can be hopeless even when the moment itself is perfectly finite.

The right power turns a constant-elasticity-of-variance (CEV) model into a squared Bessel process, and a square root turns the CIR short rate into a process with constant volatility. This article derives each of these, prices two power claims with real numbers, and then shows where the tidy picture breaks: in stochastic-volatility models, moments of a power can become infinite in finite time.

seltz.snippet:
When can a diffusion reach zero, and what happens when it does? The Feller condition as a race between drift and noise, a GBM/CIR/CEV/squared-Bessel tour, and a simulated CIR example with grid-monitoring bias.

## Boundary Behavior of Diffusion Processes

Most of the time we treat a diffusion as if it lived on the whole real line: a drift, a volatility, a Brownian shock, and off it goes. But the processes that finance actually uses are fenced in. An interest rate in the Cox-Ingersoll-Ross model cannot go negative. A stock price cannot fall below zero. A variance cannot be negative. The fence is the **boundary**, and what a diffusion does near that fence is not a technical footnote: it decides whether a rate can sit at zero, whether a stock can default inside the model, and whether your simulation is telling you the truth.

## 1. Two Questions at Every Edge

Take a one-dimensional diffusion living on an interval, almost always (0, ∞) in finance. At each end you ask two separate questions, and it pays to keep them apart.

1. **Can the process get there?** A boundary is *accessible* if the process reaches it in finite time with positive probability. It is *inaccessible* if it never does, even though it may come arbitrarily close.
1. **If it gets there, what happens next?** It might be *absorbed* (stuck forever, like a defaulted firm), *reflected* (bounced straight back into the interior), or *killed* (removed to a separate “dead” state that is not a point of the interval at all).

The first question is answered by the drift and volatility near the edge. The second is sometimes answered by the SDE itself and sometimes has to be *chosen* by the modeller, because the coefficients alone do not pin it down. Suppose someone hands you a process and asks what it is. You could try to compute its transition density, its moments, its hitting times, one property at a time. ## Regular, Exit, Entrance, and Natural Boundaries

Every one-dimensional diffusion used in finance lives on an interval. An interest rate lives on zero to infinity, a stock price lives on zero to infinity, a log-price lives on the whole real line. The ends of that interval are the **boundaries**, and William Feller showed in the 1950s that a boundary can behave in exactly four ways: **regular**, **exit**, **entrance** or **natural**. This post is a field guide to those four behaviours, organised class by class rather than model by model. For each class you get the answer to four questions: can the path reach the edge in finite time, can a path start there and leave, what must the modeller specify, and what does a textbook financial model look like when it sits in that class. Then we simulate one representative of each class and measure it.

A one-dimensional diffusion used in finance almost always lives on a half-line: an interest rate on (0, ∞), a variance on (0, ∞), a stock price on (0, ∞). At the edge you want two yes-or-no answers. Can the process **reach** the boundary in finite time? And if it were started **at** the boundary, could it **leave**? William Feller showed in the 1950s that both answers are hidden in two ordinary integrals built from the drift and volatility alone. You do not need to simulate a single path; you need to check whether two numbers are finite.

This post is about those two integrals. The intuitive picture of what boundaries do, with a tour of which models touch zero and how often, is in Boundary Behavior of Diffusion Processes. The Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) Model is a popular interest rate model used in fixed-income markets. Unlike the Vasicek Model, it ensures positive interest rates while capturing mean-reverting behavior. Learn how the CIR Model is applied in bond pricing, yield curve modeling, and risk management.

## Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) Model for Fixed Income Markets

The modelling of interest rate dynamics stands at the core of fixed income mathematics. Every bond price, every swap valuation, every swaption premium, and every regulatory capital calculation for interest rate risk depends on a model of how rates evolve through time. While the Vasicek model provided the first analytically tractable framework for interest rate dynamics, it carried a fundamental deficiency that became increasingly problematic as the field matured: it allowed interest rates to become negative with positive probability, a feature that seemed economically unreasonable in an era when nominal interest rates were universally positive.

The **Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) model**, introduced in the landmark 1985 paper \"A Theory of the Term Structure of Interest Rates\" by John Cox, Jonathan Ingersoll, and Stephen Ross, addressed this deficiency with mathematical elegance. By replacing the constant diffusion coefficient of the Vasicek model with one proportional to the square root of the short rate, CIR ensured that interest rates remain strictly positive under a well-specified parameter regime. More profoundly, the CIR model was derived from a general equilibrium framework — grounding the term structure in the optimising behaviour of a representative agent — rather than imposed as an exogenous statistical specification. This combination of economic rigour, mathematical tractability, and the non-negativity of interest rates made the CIR model one of the most influential contributions in the history of quantitative finance.

## Stochastic Processes and Their State Spaces

Every stochastic process answers two questions before it answers any interesting one: *when* is it observed, and *what values* can it take? The first is the index set, the time axis. The second is the **state space**, and it is the one most people skip. That is a mistake, because the state space is where a model quietly commits to what is possible. A short-rate model whose state space is the whole real line has already decided that negative rates can happen. A model on the positive half-line has decided they cannot. No amount of calibration later reverses that decision.

This article treats the state space as what it really is in quantitative finance: a modelling decision with consequences for boundaries, positivity, simulation and risk numbers. We finish with a fully computed comparison of the Vasicek and Cox-Ingersoll-Ross (CIR) models on the same rate, including an explicit check of the Feller condition.

That set, together with a notion of which subsets are measurable (so that we can talk about probabilities of events like “the rate is below 1%”), is the state space.
